text: So the promo code box we'll build. Our page is the promo code box of an online shop. It has a heading, a text box, and an Apply button. Under them, one of three lines can appear. There's Checking while the server checks the code. There's a red line, This code is not valid, when the server says no. And there's Code applied, You get free delivery, when the server says yes. We have no real server. Instead, a small function of ours plays the server. It waits one and a half seconds, then it says yes to the code welcome and no to every other code. Our shopper follows a very normal path. First, the shopper types welcomw, with the last letter missing, and the code is refused. Then the shopper fixes the typo to welcome, and the code is accepted. What this lesson stands on. This lesson uses these facts from earlier lessons. It's a long list, so let's go through it calmly, one lesson at a time. From lesson one: imperative and declarative. Imperative code commands each element step by step, and declarative code describes the result. From lesson two: fragments. The empty tags, the open one and the closing one, group several elements without adding an extra box to the page. From lesson three: curly braces in an attribute. They pass a JavaScript value, so disabled equals false in curly braces passes the value false, and the button works. From lesson nine: a default value for a prop. Writing status equals empty in quotes among the props gives the prop the value empty when the parent passes nothing. From lesson ten: choosing what to show. An if with an early return, the question mark and colon ternary, and the double ampersand decide what a component shows, and React creates no page element for null or false. From lesson eleven: sending a form. OnSubmit on a form runs our handler. React passes the handler an event object, e, and calling its preventDefault method stops the page from reloading. From lesson twelve: state. useState keeps a value between renders. Its setter stores a new value and asks React to draw the component again. From lesson thirteen: render and commit. After a state change, React draws the component again. Then it changes only the parts of the page that differ from last time. From lesson fifteen: waiting. setTimeout runs a function later after a wait in milliseconds. From lesson sixteen: batching. React handles the state changes of a handler after the handler's code has run. From lesson eighteen: lists. Map with a key draws one element for each item of an array. And last, from lesson twenty: a controlled box. Value equals code in curly braces makes the box show what state holds. And an onChange handler that calls setCode with the new text stores every keystroke in state. And how our project files are organized. Our project holds both versions of the promo code box. The plain page and the React page each have their own HTML file, and both use the same fake server. In figure three, we're looking at a file explorer for the project, promo code, with each file's role next to it. At the top sit the two entry files. Plain.html is the plain page, the promo form written in HTML, and it loads PlainPromo.js from the src folder. Index.html is the React page with the empty root div where React mounts. Then comes the src folder, which holds the modules. checkCode.js is the fake server. It exports checkCode, which accepts only welcome after one and a half seconds. PlainPromo.js is the plain version. It finds every element by its ID and changes it by hand. index.css holds the styles, the hidden, error, and codeBoxError classes. Main.jsx is the boundary. It imports App from App.jsx and mounts it into the root div. App.jsx is the parent. It exports App as default and imports PromoCode. And inside the components folder, PromoCode.jsx holds the state, code, and status, and draws the promo code box. So the plain page and the React page sit side by side in one project. The five principles of reacting to input with state. So let's gather it all up. A page that changes in several ways over time is hard to keep right when our code changes each element by hand. React lets us describe every look once and pick the look with state. Five practical rules follow from that. Principle one: one forgotten command breaks the page. Plain page code needs a command for every change from one look to another, and one forgotten command leaves the page in a look nobody designed. Principle two: list every look first. Before writing any logic, list every look the user can see, then draw each look from one value. Principle three: find every trigger. Some changes come from the user, others come from the computer, such as a server's answer. Both kinds must set state. Principle four: one status instead of many switches. One value that names the current look cannot be in two looks at once. Several true or false values can. And principle five: handlers only set the next state. The handler says which look comes next. The JSX already says what each look shows, and React changes the page to match. Here is the complete map of those five principles before we walk through each one. Each row of this table gives one principle, then why it matters when you debug or sit an interview, and then the React rule. Row one: one forgotten command breaks the page. Plain page code needs a command for every change from one look to another, and one forgotten command leaves the page in a look nobody designed. Row two: list every look first. Before writing any logic, list every look the user can see, then draw each look from one value. Row three: find every trigger. Some changes come from the user, others come from the computer, such as a server's answer. Both kinds must set state. Row four: one status instead of many switches. One value that names the current look cannot be in two looks at once. Several true or false values can. And principle five: handlers only set the next state. The handler says which look comes next. The JSX already says what each look shows, and React changes the page to match. A refused code and then an accepted code can leave the error line and the success line on screen together with no message in the console. The rule: describe the page for each look once and let the handler change only state. Row two: list every look first. A forgotten waiting look leaves the form working while the server checks, so an impatient shopper sends the code twice. The rule: write down every look and draw each one from one value before adding any logic. Row three: find every trigger. A handler that waits for the server but never plans for a no leaves the page stuck on its waiting look. The rule: list what the user does and what the computer does and make each one set state. Row four: one status instead of many switches. Two true or false values can both be true, so the page shows an error while the box stays off. The rule: keep one value that names the look and compute everything else from it or from other state. And row five: handlers only set the next state. Changing the page by hand inside a React component can leave a button off forever because React only changes what differs from its last render. The rule: let the handler call a setter and let the JSX decide what is shown, turned off, or styled.
